claims.assessment: His pond-side subtlety leaves no remaining traces and survives only as legend.
His hanging-curtain marvel has left almost no authentic remaining traces.
From Zhong Yao and Wang onward, calligraphy can be discussed with some confidence.
He monopolized the beauty of one generation and stood uniquely preeminent, yet whether he attained exhaustive excellence remains doubtful.
In arranging fine and thick strokes and dividing sparse and dense spacing he moves like spreading rosy clouds and rolling clouds, with nothing to obstruct him.
His style is ancient rather than modern and his characters overly long beyond the rule; these are blemishes in the great measure of his work.
His reputation exceeds his reality.
From Zhong Yao and Wang onward, calligraphy can be discussed with some confidence.
Surveying ancient and modern seal-script on silk, exhaustive goodness and exhaustive beauty belong to Wang Yishao alone.
His dots and sweeps and compositional cutting are so subtle that forms seem broken yet still linked, like mist floating and dew knotting.
His momentum is like a soaring phoenix and coiling dragon, appearing slanted yet standing straight.
One may study his writing without tiring and never know its end; heart admires and hand pursues this man alone.
All remaining calligraphers are petty and not worth discussing beside him.
Although he has his father's style, he has no fresh ingenuity.
The momentum of his characters is sparse and thin, like a withered tree in deep winter.
His brush traces are constrained, like a starving bondservant in a strict household: tethered, lean, and unfree.
The two faults together are a sickness of brush and ink.
His reputation exceeds his reality.
He recently emerged and monopolized fame south of the river, yet only achieved completed writing without a grown man's vigor: lines like spring earthworms, characters like coiled autumn snakes.
His writing is like laying Wang Meng on the paper and seating hunched Xu Yan under the brush.
Though one wear out a thousand rabbit brushes and exhaust ten thousand valleys' bark, his script gathers neither sinew nor bone.
To spread beauty by this is an inflated, undeserved reputation.
His reputation exceeds his reality.

translationRepairs: When Emperor Yuan prepared to cross south of the Yangzi, Wang Kuang had been the first to advance the plan.
When Emperor Yuan crossed south of the Yangzi, Wang Kuang had been the first to advance the plan.
The clause 元帝之過江也 sets the crossing as a narrated event; 過江 is not a still-pending preparation. The pluperfect in the replacement still allows Kuang's proposal to precede the crossing.

For years the remnant population has been bled white; shackled convicts choke the highways—policy almost as harsh as the Qin, short only of mass executions by kinship. I fear a Chen Sheng–style uprising may not be far off.

For years the remnant population has been bled white; shackled convicts choke the highways—policy almost as harsh as the Qin, short only of mass executions by kinship. I fear a Chen Sheng and Wu Guang–style uprising may not be far off.

勝廣 names both rebels; omitting Wu Guang is a real error. The proposed 'worry of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang' calques 勝廣之憂 as anxiety belonging to those men, whereas the phrase warns of a Sheng–Guang style revolt, as 無復日矣 already implies it is near.
Hopefully slowly seek the hearts of the multitude.
I hope you will gradually seek the confidence of the multitude.
幸徐求眾心 is a courteous hortative, not a fragmentary 'Hopefully slowly seek…'. The replacement restores grammar and the addressee of Yin Hao's letter.

The gone cannot be remonstrated; the coming still can be pursued; I wish the Prince again drop three thoughts, untie and restring, causing Yin Hao, Xun Xian to return and occupy Hefei, Guangling, Xuchang, Qiao commandery, Liang, Pengcheng various armies all return to guard the Huai, as foundation of invincibility; when beard root stands momentum rises, planning it is not late—this truly is of present strategies the highest.

The gone cannot be remonstrated; the coming still can be pursued; I wish the Prince again drop three thoughts, untie and restring, causing Yin Hao, Xun Xian to return and occupy Hefei, Guangling, Xuchang, Qiao commandery, Liang, Pengcheng various armies all return to guard the Huai, as foundation of invincibility; when the roots stand and momentum rises, planning it is not late—this truly is of present strategies the highest.

CText and other editions read 須根立勢舉, a wait-until-the-roots-stand metaphor after 為不可勝之基. The chapter's 鬚 yields the false calque 'beard root'; the replacement matches the intended military sense without rewriting the rest of the literal sentence.

In normal times south of the Yangzi a single capable Inspector of Yang province was enough to keep order; with so many talented men under you, disorder persists only because regulations conflict and too many hands pull in different directions. Simplify the rules so they are easy to obey, and you can preserve what we have

In normal times south of the Yangzi a single capable Inspector of Yang province was enough to keep order; with so many talented men under you, disorder persists only because regulations conflict and too many hands pull in different directions. Simplify the rules so they are easy to obey, and that will suffice to preserve the enterprise already achieved.
The inherited English stops short of 便足以保守成業. 便足以 is 'then it will suffice,' and 成業 is the enterprise already achieved, not a dangling 'what we have'.
Solidly knowing equating death and life is empty absurdity, equalizing Peng and shang is reckless making; later's viewing now, also like now's viewing past—alas!

Solidly knowing that equating death and life is empty absurdity, and that equalizing Peng Zu with a child dead young is reckless invention; later ages viewing the present are also like the present viewing the past—alas!
齊彭殤 contrasts Peng Zu with 殤, a child dead young; leaving 殤 as 'shang' and 彭 as bare 'Peng' hides that contrast, and 'reckless making' is not English for 妄作.
General-in-Chief Who Inspires Awe Wang Shu had enjoyed some fame and was ranked with Wang Xizhi, but Xizhi despised him, and the two never got along.
General of Agile Cavalry Wang Shu had enjoyed some fame and was ranked with Wang Xizhi, but Xizhi despised him, and the two never got along.
驃騎將軍 is the Agile Cavalry generalship. 'General-in-Chief Who Inspires Awe' invents a semantic title the Chinese does not carry.
Liu Dan was governor of Danyang. Xu Xun once stayed the night: fresh curtains, rich food.
Liu Tan was governor of Danyang. Xu Xun once stayed the night: fresh curtains, rich food.
劉惔 is Liu Tan; 惔 is not Dan. The surrounding 就惔宿 and 惔曰 name the same man.
At the time Liu Dan was Danyang Governor; Xu Xun once went to Dan to lodge, bed curtains new and lovely, drink and food abundant sweet.
At the time Liu Tan was Danyang Governor; Xu Xun once went to Tan to lodge, bed curtains new and lovely, drink and food abundant sweet.
The same 惔 is the host of 就惔宿; rendering him twice as Dan is a naming error in the literal field.
He died at fifty-nine and was posthumously honored as Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
Wang Xizhi died at fifty-nine and was posthumously honored as Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
After 萬不能用，果敗, English 'He died' would attach to Xie Wan. 年五十九卒 and the following 諸子…子凝之 resume Wang Xizhi's biography.
His sons, obeying his earlier wishes, firmly declined the enfeoffment.
His sons, obeying his earlier wishes, firmly declined the posthumous honor.
固讓不受 continues 贈金紫光祿大夫, a posthumous honor, not an enfeoffment.
He later served as cavalry adviser to Huan Chong, the Cavalry-in-Attendant. Huan Chong asked, "Which section are you attached to?"
He later served as cavalry adviser to Huan Chong, the General of Chariot and Cavalry. Huan Chong asked, "Which section are you attached to?"
車騎桓沖 is Huan Chong titled by the Chariot-and-Cavalry generalship (車騎將軍), distinct from the 騎兵參軍 post Huizhi held. Cavalry-in-Attendant is the wrong office.

He later served as a Palace Attendant, then quit and went east. He and Xianzhi both lay near death when a occultist said, "When a man's span is up, if another willingly trades his years, the dying man may live."

He later served as a Palace Attendant, then quit and went east. He and Xianzhi both lay near death when an occultist said, "When a man's span is up, if another willingly trades his years, the dying man may live."
'A occultist' is ungrammatical English before a vowel-initial noun; the Chinese 術人 is unchanged.
The heading 子操之 resumes Wang Xizhi's sons after Huizhi's cadet line (楨之). 'His son' after Zhenzhi's speech would make Caozhi Zhenzhi's child, which 子操之 does not say.
子獻之 is the next brother-heading under Xizhi, not Caozhi's son; treating Xianzhi as Caozhi's child is a kinship error.

When Empress Anxi was installed, her father Wang Xianzhi was posthumously honored as Palace Attendant, Specially Advanced, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, and Grand Governor with the posthumous title "Xian."

When Empress Anxi was installed, her father Wang Xianzhi was posthumously honored as Palace Attendant, Specially Advanced, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, and Grand Steward, with the posthumous title "Xian."
太宰 is Grand Steward. Grand Governor is a wrong office name for the posthumous grant listed after 光祿大夫.
Your Majesty ascended the throne; yang-autumn still plentiful, exhausting heart and exhausting wisdom to assist sagely brightness.
Your Majesty ascended the throne; his years were still plentiful, exhausting heart and exhausting wisdom to assist sagely brightness.
陽秋尚富 is the Jin taboo writing of 春秋尚富, 'years still plentiful,' of Xie An who then 盡心竭智以輔聖明. The calque 'yang-autumn' hides that age/prime sense.
The historian's judgment runs: Writing arose in high antiquity from knotted cords and bird-track glyphs—scarcely worth our notice.
The historian's judgment runs: The rise of writing began in middle antiquity; knotted-cord patterns and bird-track glyphs are scarcely worth our notice.
肇乎中古 is middle antiquity, not high antiquity. 繩文鳥跡，不足可觀 is a separate dismissal of knotted-cord and bird-track graphs, not the origin identified with 書契之興.
Only from Zhong Yao and the Wangs onward can one speak with confidence.
Only from Zhong Yao and Wang onward can one speak with confidence.
鐘王 is the pair Zhong and Wang (Xizhi), continued by 鐘雖擅美一時. Plural 'the Wangs' invents a clan where the text names one Wang.
Combining these two, therefore brush-ink's sickness sucks!
Combining these two, therefore it is a sickness of brush and ink!
CText reads 故翰墨之病歟, a rhetorical close. Translating chapter 歙 as the English verb 'sucks' is a false reading; the sentence names the two faults as a sickness of brush and ink.
